items.title: From paper folders to electronic health records
objectives: Define health informatics as the meeting point of people, information and technology
Distinguish an electronic medical record, an electronic health record and a personal health record
Identify the main users of an EHR and what each needs from it
Weigh the main benefits and challenges of moving from paper to electronic records
chips: What is the difference between an EMR and an EHR?
Why can a paper folder be dangerous in an emergency?
Who besides doctors uses the electronic health record?

chapters.title: The folder that went missing

cards.label: Regional hospital
cards.text: Admission notes and an allergy written in red

note.text: A hypothetical Mauritian scenario used throughout the course

narration: Picture a sixty-eight-year-old woman with diabetes who collapses at a bus stop in Port Louis and is rushed to the emergency department of a regional public hospital.

Her blood pressure readings live in a paper folder at her area health centre in Rose-Hill, her last blood test sits in a private laboratory, and her penicillin allergy is written in red ink on a hospital folder from three years ago.
The emergency doctor has none of these in front of her. She has to decide on treatment while the information that could guide her is scattered across three buildings.
This is the everyday problem that health informatics sets out to solve. Information exists, but it is not in the right place, in the right form, at the right moment.
Over the next twelve weeks we will look at how electronic records, data standards and privacy safeguards work together so that this patient gets safer care.

chapters.title: What health informatics is

slide.heading: Health informatics: three ingredients
points: People: patients, clinicians, managers, public health teams
Information: what is recorded, how, and what it means
Goal: better, safer, more efficient care

narration: Health informatics is the discipline that studies how health information is collected, stored, shared and used to improve care.
I like to describe it as the meeting point of three things: people, information and technology. If you forget any one of the three, projects fail.
A beautifully designed computer system that nurses find too slow to use at the bedside will simply be bypassed, and the information will end up back on scraps of paper.
So as future health professionals, you do not need to become programmers. You need to understand what good health information looks like and how systems help or hinder your work.
That is exactly the level this course is pitched at, practical and clinical rather than deeply technical.
Throughout the course I will keep asking a simple question: does this help the right person get the right information at the right time, without exposing it to the wrong person?

chapters.title: EMR, EHR and PHR
narration: You will meet three terms that people often mix up. An electronic medical record is the digital chart held by a single organisation, such as one clinic or one hospital.
An electronic health record goes further. It aims to be a longitudinal record of a person's health across many settings and over time, shared with the authorised professionals who care for them.
A personal health record is controlled by the patient, for example a mobile app where someone logs their blood glucose and chooses what to share with their doctor.
In practice the words are used loosely, but the key idea is reach. An electronic health record is designed to travel with the patient between the health centre, the hospital and the laboratory.
Notice that our collapsed patient would have been helped most by exactly that kind of record.

chapters.title: Who uses the record, and why

cards.label: Public health
cards.text: Disease trends such as dengue cases

narration: The electronic record is not only a clinical notebook. Doctors and nurses use it for history, results and care plans, but many other people depend on it too.
Pharmacists check prescriptions against allergies and other medicines. Laboratory staff send results into it. Managers use summary data to plan beds, staff and drug stock.
Public health teams use aggregated data to spot trends, for instance a rise in dengue cases after heavy summer rains, so that vector control can be targeted quickly.
And increasingly, patients themselves want to see their results and appointments online. Each of these users needs a different view of the same underlying data.
That is an important design principle we will come back to when we discuss access control: different roles should see different slices of the record.
Even the cleaner and the porter may appear in the workflow, for example when a bed is marked as ready, but they should see nothing clinical.

chapters.title: Benefits and challenges

note.text: Technology alone does not guarantee safer care

narration: The benefits are real. Records become legible and available around the clock, computers can warn about allergies and drug interactions, and managers get data instead of guesswork.
But there are challenges. Systems cost money, staff need training, power cuts and network failures during a cyclone can make records unavailable, and badly designed screens slow clinicians down.
Too many warnings cause alert fatigue, where busy staff click through every pop-up without reading it, which can be as dangerous as having no warnings at all.
And when records are electronic and shared, a single breach can expose thousands of patients at once. That is why privacy is one of the three pillars of this course.

chapters.title: Recap

slide.heading: Key points
points: Informatics joins people, information and technology
An EHR is longitudinal and shared across settings
Many users need different views of one record
Benefits come with usability, downtime and privacy risks

narration: To recap, health informatics is about getting the right information to the right person at the right time, and it depends on people as much as technology.
An electronic health record differs from a single clinic's chart because it follows the patient across settings and is shared with authorised professionals.
Next, in our interactive lesson, we will open up an electronic health record and look at the components inside it.

items.title: Inside an electronic health record: the core components
objectives: Explain how an EHR differs from a scanned paper record
Describe the core components of an EHR and how they work together
Explain why coded terminologies matter for EHR data
chips: What is clinical decision support?

summary: An EHR holds structured, shared data, not pictures of paper
Components such as the allergy list, order entry and decision support work together

segments.title: More than a scanned folder
speech: Some hospitals begin their digital journey by scanning old paper folders. That is useful for storage, but a scanned page is only a picture of handwriting.
In a true electronic health record, a blood pressure is stored as numbers in a defined field, a diagnosis as a code, and a medicine with its dose and frequency. That is what we call structured data.
Because the data is structured, the computer can search it, draw a graph of a patient's blood glucose over a year, and check a new prescription against known allergies.
And because the record is shared, the nurse on the ward, the pharmacist and the doctor in clinic can all open the same up-to-date record at the same time, wherever they are authorised to work.
simpler: Let me put it more simply. A scanned folder is like a photo of a page. You can look at it, but the computer cannot understand it.
An electronic health record is more like a spreadsheet that the computer understands, so it can search, sort and warn.
And instead of one folder on one shelf, everyone who is allowed can open the same record from wherever they are.

segments.title: The core components and how they connect

cards.label: Medications and orders
cards.text: Electronic prescribing, lab and imaging orders

speech: Most EHRs share a common set of components. Demographics identify the patient. The problem list and allergy list summarise what matters most clinically.
The medication list and order entry let clinicians prescribe and request tests electronically, often called computerised provider order entry. Results flow back from the laboratory and radiology.
Clinical notes capture the story: consultations, nursing observations and discharge summaries. Around all of this sits clinical decision support, which applies rules to the data.
The power comes from the connections. When a doctor orders a medicine, decision support checks it against the allergy list and the other medicines, and raises an alert if there is a problem.
simpler: Think of the EHR as a house with several rooms: a room for who you are, a room for your allergies, a room for your medicines, and a room for your test results.
Decision support is like a careful housekeeper who walks between the rooms and notices when something does not fit.
If a new medicine arrives that clashes with an allergy, the housekeeper raises the alarm before any harm is done.

checkpoint.question: A doctor at an area health centre starts to prescribe amoxicillin for a patient whose record lists a penicillin allergy. Which parts of the EHR work together to catch this, and how?
checkpoint.ack: That is it: the recorded allergy in the allergy list is checked by clinical decision support against the new medication order, which raises an alert before the prescription is signed.

segments.title: Why codes matter

cards.label: ICD-10
cards.text: Classifying diagnoses for statistics and reporting

cards.label: SNOMED CT
cards.text: Detailed clinical terms for the record

note.text: Free text is still useful for the narrative, but codes make data computable

speech: Free text is natural for clinicians, but one doctor writes type 2 diabetes, another writes T2DM, and a third writes diabetes, non insulin dependent.
Standard terminologies solve this. ICD-10 classifies diagnoses for statistics, SNOMED CT offers detailed clinical terms, and LOINC identifies laboratory tests such as glycated haemoglobin.
When a diagnosis carries a standard code, it means exactly the same thing in every record and every system, so the computer can search for it and count it reliably.
That is how a health ministry can produce accurate figures on diabetes across all its clinics, and, as we will see next module, how systems can exchange data without losing meaning.
simpler: Think of a barcode on a packet of rice. The label might be written in different ways, but the barcode is always the same.
A terminology code is a barcode for a diagnosis or a test.
Because the barcode never changes, the computer can count and find things without getting confused.

checkpoint.question: Optional check: Why is it better to record a diagnosis with a code from a standard terminology rather than only as free text?
checkpoint.ack: Well put: a standard code means exactly the same thing everywhere, so computers can reliably search, count and analyse it.

closing: Let me summarise what we covered.
An electronic health record holds structured, shared data that the computer can search and act on, which is what makes it more than a scanned folder.
Its components, such as the allergy list, order entry and decision support, work together to catch errors, and coded terminologies make the data consistent and countable.
For revision, read the next article on the anatomy of an EHR, and then we will move on to how records are exchanged between systems. Well done.

items.title: Anatomy of an EHR: components, workflow and data quality
objectives: List the core functional components of an electronic health record
Trace how data moves through the EHR during a typical patient visit
Explain the main dimensions of health-data quality
Recognise how poor data quality can harm patients
chips: What is the difference between a problem list and a diagnosis?
Why is a master patient index important?
What does data completeness mean in an EHR?
items.body:
An electronic health record (EHR) is often described as "the patient's chart on a computer", but that description undersells it. A modern EHR is a collection of linked functional components, each with its own data and its own users, connected by a single patient identity. In this reading we open up those components, follow a patient through a typical visit, and examine why the *quality* of the data matters as much as the software that holds it.

## The core components

Different vendors package things differently, but almost every EHR contains the following building blocks.

| Component | What it holds | Typical users |
|---|---|---|
| Patient demographics and identity | Name, date of birth, sex, address, contacts, national identifier | Registration clerks, all clinicians |
| Problem list | Active and past diagnoses, often coded | Doctors, nurses |
| Allergy and alert list | Drug and food allergies, other safety alerts | Doctors, pharmacists, nurses |
| Medication list and e-prescribing | Current medicines, doses, prescriptions | Doctors, pharmacists |
| Order entry | Requests for laboratory tests, imaging, referrals | Doctors, nurses |
| Results | Laboratory values, imaging reports | Clinicians, laboratory staff |
| Clinical notes | Consultation, nursing, discharge notes | All clinicians |
| Clinical decision support | Rules, alerts, reminders, care pathways | Works in the background |
| Administrative functions | Appointments, admissions, bed management | Clerks, managers |

Two components deserve special attention.

### The master patient index

Every other component hangs off the patient's identity. A **master patient index** (MPI) makes sure that "Marie Claire Lebon, born 1958" registered at a health centre is recognised as the same person when she arrives at a regional hospital. If identity matching fails, the system creates a duplicate record, and the allergy recorded in one copy is invisible from the other. In a country that issues a national identity card, the identifier helps, but clinics still need rules for patients who arrive without documents, such as visitors or unconscious patients.

### Clinical decision support

Clinical decision support (CDS) applies knowledge to patient data. Simple examples include a drug–allergy alert, a dose check for children based on weight, or a reminder that a diabetic patient is due for an annual eye examination. CDS is only as good as the data it reads: if the allergy was typed into a free-text note instead of the allergy list, the rule will never fire.

## Following a patient through the record

> **Worked example: a diabetes review at a hypothetical area health centre**
>
> 1. **Registration.** The clerk searches the MPI using the patient's national identifier and confirms address and phone number. The appointment is marked as arrived.
> 2. **Triage.** A nurse records weight, blood pressure and a finger-prick glucose into structured fields. The system plots the blood pressure against the last four visits.
> 3. **Consultation.** The doctor reviews the problem list (type 2 diabetes, hypertension), sees that the last HbA1c result from the laboratory was high, and writes a short note.
> 4. **Orders.** The doctor increases the metformin dose through e-prescribing and orders a repeat HbA1c. Decision support checks the dose against kidney function results and raises no alert.
> 5. **Results.** A week later the laboratory system sends the HbA1c result back into the record, where it appears in the results view and triggers a task for the doctor to review it.
> 6. **Reporting.** At the end of the month, coded diagnoses and results from all visits are aggregated, without names, into a report on diabetes control across the region.

Notice how each step both *uses* and *creates* data, and how the value at step 6 depends on careful recording at steps 1 to 5.

## Data quality: the hidden foundation

Clinicians sometimes say "rubbish in, rubbish out". Health informatics uses a more precise vocabulary. The most widely used dimensions of data quality are:

- **Accuracy**: the data correctly describes reality. A weight of 7 kg recorded for an adult is clearly an error.
- **Completeness**: the required data is present. An allergy list that is simply empty is ambiguous; good systems distinguish "no known allergies" from "not yet asked".
- **Timeliness**: data is recorded and available when needed. A result that arrives after the patient has left may never be acted on.
- **Consistency**: the same fact is recorded the same way in different places. Coded terminologies such as ICD-10, SNOMED CT and LOINC are a major tool here.
- **Validity**: values follow the agreed format and range, such as dates in a valid format or blood pressure within plausible limits.
- **Uniqueness**: each patient has one record, not several duplicates.

### Why poor quality is a safety issue

Data quality is not just an administrative concern. A duplicate record can hide an allergy; a missing unit can turn 5 mg into 5 g; a result filed against the wrong patient can lead to treatment for a disease the patient does not have. At population level, poor coding distorts statistics, so a ministry might under-estimate the burden of hypertension and under-order medicines.

## Designing for good data

Good data quality comes from a combination of system design and professional habits:

1. **Structured entry where it matters.** Allergies, medicines and vital signs belong in structured fields, while the clinical narrative can remain free text.
2. **Validation at the point of entry.** The system can reject impossible values or ask the user to confirm unusual ones.
3. **Sensible defaults and pick-lists.** Choosing from a coded list is faster and more consistent than typing, provided the list is well designed.
4. **Feedback to staff.** When teams see the reports built from their data, they understand why accuracy matters.
5. **Avoiding copy-and-paste.** Copying yesterday's note forward is convenient but can carry outdated or wrong information into today's record.

Usability is part of quality. If recording an allergy takes eight clicks, busy staff will find a shortcut, and the shortcut is usually a free-text note that decision support cannot read.

## Key takeaways

- An EHR is a set of linked components (identity, problems, allergies, medications, orders, results, notes and decision support) sharing one patient identity.
- The master patient index prevents duplicate records that could hide vital information.
- Clinical decision support only works when the data it needs is recorded in the right structured place.
- Data quality has several dimensions: accuracy, completeness, timeliness, consistency, validity and uniqueness.
- Poor data quality is a patient-safety issue as well as a reporting problem.

## Check your understanding

1. Why might an allergy recorded only in a free-text consultation note fail to protect a patient?
*Answer:* Decision support rules read the structured allergy list, so an allergy hidden in free text will not trigger an alert when a conflicting medicine is ordered.
2. A clinic's report shows far fewer hypertension cases than expected. Name two data-quality dimensions that might explain this.
*Answer:* Completeness (diagnoses not recorded) and consistency (diagnoses recorded in free text or with different codes so they are not counted).
3. What is the role of the master patient index?
*Answer:* It links all records belonging to the same person and prevents duplicates, so information recorded in one setting is visible in another.

items.title: Interoperability: why health systems need to talk to each other
objectives: Define interoperability in health care
Distinguish structural and semantic interoperability
Outline the evolution of HL7 standards from version 2 to FHIR
Explain the role of terminologies in exchanging meaning
chips: What is semantic interoperability?
Why did HL7 create FHIR when version 2 already existed?
How does LOINC help when exchanging lab results?

chapters.title: Islands of information
narration: Mauritius is an island nation, and health data has a habit of behaving like a set of islands too. Each clinic, laboratory and hospital may run its own computer system.
A laboratory information system is excellent at managing samples. A hospital system is good at admissions and wards. A pharmacy system tracks dispensing. But each was built for its own job.
If these systems cannot exchange data, clinicians fall back on printing results, faxing letters and retyping information, which is slow and introduces errors.
Interoperability is the ability of different systems and organisations to exchange data and to use the data they receive. Those last few words, use the data, are the important part.
Think of our patient from week one. Her laboratory result was correct, but it was trapped in the wrong system, so it could not help the doctor who needed it.

chapters.title: Levels of interoperability

steps.title: Foundational
steps.sub: Data can be sent and received

narration: It helps to think of interoperability in levels. The foundational level simply means one system can send data and the other can receive it, like posting a letter.
Structural interoperability means both sides agree on the format, so the receiving system knows which part is the patient's name and which part is the test result.
Semantic interoperability goes further. Both systems agree on what the data means, usually by using shared codes, so a glucose result from one laboratory is recognised as the same test everywhere.

Finally, organisational interoperability covers the policies, agreements and trust between institutions, including who is allowed to see what, and under what consent. Technology alone cannot deliver this level.
In practice, most failures happen at the semantic and organisational levels, not because data cannot travel, but because nobody agreed what it means or who may use it.

chapters.title: A short history of HL7
narration: The most important standards body in this area is HL7 International. HL7 stands for Health Level Seven, a reference to the application layer in a classic networking model.
HL7 version 2, first released in the late nineteen eighties, defined text messages with fields separated by vertical bar characters. It is still used in laboratories and hospitals all over the world.

Its weakness was flexibility. Every hospital interpreted it slightly differently, so each new interface needed custom work. People joked that if you have seen one version two interface, you have seen one version two interface.
Later came the Clinical Document Architecture, which packages whole documents such as discharge summaries. And then, in the twenty tens, HL7 developed FHIR, which we will study in detail next.
Version two is not going away soon. Many hospitals run version two interfaces for laboratory orders and results alongside newer FHIR services, and integration engines translate between them.

chapters.title: Why FHIR appeared

slide.heading: What FHIR set out to fix
points: Use ordinary web technology developers already know
Break health data into small, reusable resources
Support apps, mobile phones and cloud services
Make the basics simple and allow extensions

narration: FHIR, pronounced fire, stands for Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources. It was designed to use the same web technology that powers online banking and shopping apps.
Instead of one huge message, FHIR breaks health information into small building blocks called resources, such as a Patient, an Observation or an Encounter.
Systems exchange these resources through a web interface called a RESTful API, usually in JSON format, which any modern programmer can read.
That lowered the barrier enormously. A small team building a mobile app for a diabetes clinic can now connect to a hospital system without learning a decades-old message format.

Another important design choice is that FHIR focuses on the common cases. Rather than modelling everything, it covers what most systems need, and lets countries add local requirements through extensions.
A widely implemented release is called R4, and newer releases continue to be published, so projects always state which version they build on.

chapters.title: Terminologies carry the meaning

cards.label: FHIR
cards.text: Defines the structure: which field is which

cards.label: SNOMED CT
cards.text: Says which clinical finding or problem

cards.label: UCUM
cards.text: Says which unit, such as millimoles per litre

note.text: A well-formed message with the wrong code is still wrong

narration: A standard like FHIR gives us structural interoperability: everyone agrees where the result goes. But we still need semantic interoperability: everyone agrees what the result is.
That is the job of terminologies. LOINC codes identify laboratory tests and observations, SNOMED CT identifies clinical findings and procedures, and units come from a standard called UCUM.
So a glucose value travelling from a private laboratory to a public health centre carries a LOINC code saying which test it was, the number itself, and a standard unit.
Without those codes, the receiving system sees only a number and a label it may not recognise, and we are back to a human reading and retyping.

chapters.title: Recap

slide.heading: Key points
points: Interoperability means exchanging and using data
Structural agrees on format; semantic agrees on meaning
Terminologies such as LOINC and SNOMED CT carry meaning

narration: To recap, interoperability is about exchanging data and being able to use it, and it works at foundational, structural, semantic and organisational levels.
HL7 standards evolved from version two messages to documents and then to FHIR resources, while terminologies like LOINC and SNOMED CT make sure the meaning survives the journey.
In the next reading we will open up FHIR resources and look at what is inside them.

items.title: HL7 FHIR resources explained
objectives: Describe what a FHIR resource is and how it is structured
Identify common resources such as Patient, Observation and Encounter
Read a simple FHIR resource in JSON
Explain how references link resources together
chips: What does resourceType mean in a FHIR JSON file?
How does an Observation point to its patient?
What is a FHIR profile?
items.body:
HL7 **FHIR** (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is the newest family of HL7 standards and the one you are most likely to meet in new health IT projects. You do not need to be a programmer to understand it. At its heart, FHIR is a catalogue of agreed building blocks, called **resources**, and a set of rules for exchanging them over the web. This reading explains what resources are, introduces the ones you will meet most often, and walks through a worked example from a hypothetical Mauritian health centre.

## What is a resource?

A resource is a small, self-contained unit of health information with a defined structure. Each resource type describes one kind of "thing" in health care: a person, an event, a measurement, a medicine order. The FHIR specification defines around 150 resource types, but a small core covers most everyday needs.

Every resource has:

- a **resourceType**, such as `Patient` or `Observation`, which tells the receiver what kind of thing it is;
- an **id**, the identifier of that resource on the server that holds it;
- a set of **elements** (fields) defined by the specification, such as `birthDate` for a Patient or `valueQuantity` for an Observation;
- optional **metadata**, such as when it was last updated;
- usually a short human-readable **narrative**, so a person can still read the content.

Resources can be represented in JSON or XML. JSON is the most common choice for modern web and mobile applications.

## Resources you will meet most often

| Resource | Represents | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Patient` | Demographic details of a person receiving care | Name, date of birth, national identifier |
| `Practitioner` | A health professional | A medical officer at a health centre |
| `Organization` | A hospital, clinic, laboratory or ministry | A regional public hospital |
| `Encounter` | An interaction between patient and provider | An outpatient visit or an admission |
| `Observation` | A measurement or finding | Blood pressure, HbA1c, smoking status |
| `Condition` | A problem or diagnosis | Type 2 diabetes |
| `AllergyIntolerance` | An allergy or intolerance | Penicillin allergy |
| `MedicationRequest` | A prescription or medication order | Metformin 500 mg twice daily |

Notice how closely these map to the EHR components you studied earlier: the problem list becomes a set of `Condition` resources, the allergy list a set of `AllergyIntolerance` resources, results become `Observation` resources, and so on.

## Reading a resource in JSON

Here is a simplified `Patient` resource for a fictional patient:

```json
{
  "resourceType": "Patient",
  "id": "pat-1024",
  "identifier": [
    { "system": "urn:example:mu-national-id", "value": "L0101580000000" }
  ],
  "name": [ { "family": "Lebon", "given": ["Marie", "Claire"] } ],
  "gender": "female",
  "birthDate": "1958-03-14"
}
```

Even without any programming knowledge you can read it: it is a Patient, its server id is `pat-1024`, it carries an identifier from a (made-up) national identifier system, and it has a name, gender and date of birth. Curly brackets group the elements of an object, square brackets hold lists, because a patient can have more than one name or identifier.

## References: linking resources together

Resources rarely stand alone. An Observation is *about* a patient and usually happened *during* an encounter. FHIR expresses these links with **references**, which point from one resource to another.

> **Worked example: a blood glucose result at a hypothetical health centre**
>
> A nurse measures a fasting blood glucose during an outpatient visit. The system creates an `Encounter` for the visit and an `Observation` for the result:
>
> ```json
> {
>   "resourceType": "Observation",
>   "id": "obs-5531",
>   "status": "final",
>   "code": {
>     "coding": [ { "system": "http://loinc.org", "code": "1558-6",
>                   "display": "Fasting glucose [Moles/volume] in Serum or Plasma" } ]
>   },
>   "subject": { "reference": "Patient/pat-1024" },
>   "encounter": { "reference": "Encounter/enc-778" },
>   "effectiveDateTime": "2026-02-10T08:40:00+04:00",
>   "valueQuantity": { "value": 7.8, "unit": "mmol/L",
>                      "system": "http://unitsofmeasure.org", "code": "mmol/L" }
> }
> ```
>
> Read it piece by piece. The `code` uses a LOINC code to say *which* test was done. The `subject` points to the Patient resource. The `encounter` links it to the visit. The `valueQuantity` carries the number with a UCUM unit. The `+04:00` in the time is Mauritius time. Any FHIR-capable system receiving this knows exactly what was measured, for whom, when and in what unit.

The `status` element matters too: `final` means the result is confirmed, whereas `preliminary` would warn the reader that it might still change.

## Terminology bindings, profiles and extensions

FHIR deliberately keeps resources general so they work in any country. Three mechanisms let them be tailored:

1. **Terminology bindings** say which code system an element should use, for example LOINC for laboratory Observation codes or SNOMED CT for Conditions.
2. **Profiles** are rules that constrain a resource for a particular use, such as "in our national programme, every Patient must carry a national identifier". A set of profiles for one country or project is published as an **implementation guide**.
3. **Extensions** add elements the base specification does not include, such as a locally required field, in a standard way that other systems can safely ignore.

A ministry planning national health data exchange would typically publish its own implementation guide, so that every vendor builds to the same profiles.

## Bundles: sending several resources together

Sometimes you need to send many resources at once, such as a patient, an encounter and five observations from a single visit, or the results of a search. FHIR wraps them in a **Bundle** resource. You will see Bundles again when we look at searching a FHIR server through its API.

## Key takeaways

- FHIR breaks health information into small, well-defined building blocks called resources.
- Every resource has a `resourceType`, an id and defined elements, and is usually exchanged as JSON.
- Core resources include `Patient`, `Practitioner`, `Organization`, `Encounter`, `Observation`, `Condition`, `AllergyIntolerance` and `MedicationRequest`.
- References such as `"subject": {"reference": "Patient/pat-1024"}` link resources together.
- Terminologies give meaning; profiles and implementation guides tailor FHIR to a country or project.

## Check your understanding

1. Which FHIR resource would you use to record a patient's blood pressure reading?
*Answer:* An `Observation`, with a code identifying blood pressure and the measured values.
2. In the glucose example, how does the receiving system know which patient the result belongs to?
*Answer:* The `subject` element contains a reference to the Patient resource, `Patient/pat-1024`.
3. What is the purpose of a FHIR profile?
*Answer:* It constrains a general resource for a specific use, for example making a national identifier mandatory, so that all systems in a programme record data in the same way.

items.title: FHIR in action: the RESTful API and JSON
objectives: Explain what a RESTful API is in plain terms
Match the main HTTP operations to FHIR interactions
Describe how a FHIR search returns a Bundle
Recognise how access to a FHIR server is secured
chips: What does GET do in a FHIR API?
What is a Bundle in a search result?
What is SMART on FHIR?

chapters.title: Ordering from a menu

slide.heading: An API is a menu
points: A client asks, a server answers
Answers usually come back as JSON

narration: In the last reading we looked inside FHIR resources. Now let us see how systems actually ask for them and send them.
An application programming interface, or API, is like a menu in a restaurant. You do not walk into the kitchen. You order from a fixed list, in an agreed way, and the kitchen sends back your dish.
In FHIR, the client might be a mobile app at a diabetes clinic and the server might be the hospital's FHIR server. The app sends a request over the internet, and the server replies with resources.
FHIR uses a style called REST, which simply means it uses the same web addresses and operations that your browser already uses every day.
The good news for you as clinicians is that you will rarely type these requests yourselves. But understanding them helps you talk to the technical teams who build your systems.

chapters.title: Resources have addresses
narration: In a RESTful API, every resource has its own web address. It is built from three parts: the base address of the server, the resource type, and the id of that particular resource.
So to fetch the patient with id pat one zero two four, the app asks for the base address followed by slash Patient slash pat one zero two four.
To fetch a particular observation, it uses Observation followed by its id in exactly the same way. Once you have seen the pattern, it is easy to predict.
This predictability is a big part of FHIR's appeal. Developers from banking or tourism apps already understand the pattern, so they can start working with health data quickly.
The base address is set by the organisation. A ministry might run one national FHIR server, or each hospital might have its own, connected through an exchange service.

chapters.title: The four everyday operations
narration: The web uses a handful of operations, and FHIR maps its interactions onto them. GET means read. When the app sends a GET request for a Patient address, the server returns that patient.
POST means create. When a nurse records a new blood pressure on a tablet, the app posts a new Observation resource to the server, which stores it and gives it an id.
PUT means update, for example correcting a patient's phone number. And DELETE removes a resource, although in health care deletion is often restricted, because records must be kept.
Each reply also carries a status code. Two hundred means success, two hundred and one means created, and four hundred and four means not found, the same codes your browser sees.
There is also PATCH, for changing just part of a resource, but the four we have mentioned are enough to understand how almost every FHIR application works.

chapters.title: Searching and Bundles

slide.heading: A FHIR search and its reply
points: Matches come back inside a Bundle

narration: Often we do not know the id. We want, say, all the glycated haemoglobin results for one patient. FHIR supports this with search parameters added to the address.
The app asks the Observation endpoint for observations where the patient is pat one zero two four and the code is the LOINC code for haemoglobin A one c.
The server replies with a Bundle, a container resource of type search set. It says how many matches there were, and holds each matching Observation as an entry.
The app can then draw a graph of the patient's diabetes control over time, which is exactly the kind of feature a clinic dashboard needs.
Searches can combine parameters such as date ranges, so a clinic can ask only for results from the last twelve months, which keeps the reply small and relevant.

chapters.title: Reading the JSON and keeping it secure

slide.heading: JSON and security
points: JSON: names and values in curly brackets
resourceType tells you what you are reading
SMART on FHIR uses OAuth 2.0 for authorisation

note.text: An open API without authorisation would be a privacy disaster

narration: The replies come back as JSON, short for JavaScript Object Notation. It is simply pairs of names and values, such as resource type Patient, or birth date nineteen fifty-eight.
Because health data is so sensitive, a FHIR server must never be open to anyone who knows the address. Traffic is encrypted, and every request must be authorised.
A widely used approach is SMART on FHIR, which builds on the OAuth two point zero standard. The user logs in, and the app receives a token that limits what it may read or write.

For example, a patient app might be allowed to read only that patient's own observations, while a clinician's app can read the records of patients under their care. This links directly to our privacy module.

chapters.title: Recap

slide.heading: Key points
points: Every resource has a predictable web address
GET reads, POST creates, PUT updates, DELETE removes
Searches return a Bundle of matching resources
Access is encrypted and authorised, for example with SMART on FHIR

narration: To recap, FHIR exposes resources through a RESTful API, where each resource has a predictable address and ordinary web operations read, create, update or delete it.
Searches return Bundles, data travels as JSON, and security standards such as SMART on FHIR control who can access what.
Next you will test yourself on records and FHIR in the first quiz.

items.title: Quiz 1: Electronic health records and FHIR

questions.q: Which feature most clearly distinguishes an electronic health record from an electronic medical record?
o: It is stored in the cloud
It is longitudinal and shared across care settings
It is controlled entirely by the patient
questions.ex: An EHR aims to follow the patient across organisations and over time, whereas an EMR is one organisation's chart.

questions.q: A patient's penicillin allergy was typed only into a free-text consultation note. Why might the EHR fail to warn a doctor who prescribes amoxicillin?
o: Decision support reads the structured allergy list, not free-text notes
Amoxicillin is not related to penicillin
Free-text notes are deleted after each visit
Allergy alerts only work for hospital inpatients
questions.ex: Decision support rules run on structured, coded data, so an allergy hidden in free text does not trigger the alert.

questions.q: A clinic finds that one patient has three separate records. Which component is designed to prevent this?
questions.ex: The master patient index matches and links records belonging to the same person, preventing duplicates.

questions.q: Two systems exchange a lab result in an agreed format, but one uses a local code the other does not recognise. Which level of interoperability is missing?
questions.ex: Semantic interoperability requires shared meaning, usually through common codes such as LOINC.

questions.q: Which FHIR resource is most appropriate for recording a patient's HbA1c result?
questions.ex: Measurements and test results are represented as Observation resources.

questions.q: In a FHIR Observation, what does the element "subject": {"reference": "Patient/pat-1024"} do?
o: Links the observation to the patient it is about
Records which clinician measured the value
questions.ex: A reference in the subject element points to the Patient resource the observation describes.

questions.q: A clinic app needs to create a new blood pressure Observation on a FHIR server. Which HTTP operation does it normally use?
questions.ex: POST to the resource type endpoint creates a new resource; GET reads or searches.

questions.q: An app searches GET [base]/Observation?patient=pat-1024. What type of resource does the server return?
questions.ex: FHIR search results are returned as a Bundle of type searchset holding the matching entries.

items.title: Core principles of health-data privacy
objectives: Distinguish privacy, confidentiality and security
Explain consent and purpose limitation in health care
Apply data minimisation and need-to-know access to clinical scenarios
Explain why audit trails underpin accountability
chips: What is the difference between privacy and security?
What does data minimisation mean in a clinic?
Is consent always needed to share data for treatment?

chapters.title: Why health data is special

slide.heading: Why health data needs extra care

cards.label: Intimate
cards.text: Diagnoses, sexual and mental health, genetics

cards.label: Permanent
cards.text: You cannot change your medical history like a password

cards.label: Small island
cards.text: In a small community, people are easily recognised

narration: Imagine a nurse at a district hospital who notices that a neighbour has been admitted, opens his record out of curiosity, and mentions his diagnosis at a family wedding.
No hacker was involved, no system failed, yet a serious breach of privacy has happened, and the patient may lose trust in the health service altogether.
Health data is special. It can reveal mental illness, sexual health, pregnancy or genetic risk. Once it is exposed it cannot be changed like a password.
In a small island community, where people often know each other, even a few details such as age, village and diagnosis can identify a person. That makes careful handling even more important.
Patients who fear that their information will leak may hide symptoms or avoid care altogether, which harms their own health and, for infectious diseases, the health of the community.

chapters.title: Privacy, confidentiality and security

columns.title: Confidentiality
points: not to disclose what you learn

narration: Three words are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things. Privacy is the patient's right to control how information about them is collected and used.
Confidentiality is the duty that health professionals owe patients: what you learn in the course of care is not disclosed without a proper reason. It is as old as the Hippocratic tradition.
Security is the set of safeguards, such as passwords, encryption, locked rooms and backups, that protect data from unauthorised access, loss or damage.
You can have strong security and still breach privacy, as our curious nurse shows. She had a valid login; she simply had no legitimate reason to use it.
In practice we need all three working together. Security protects the data, confidentiality guides professional behaviour, and respect for privacy shapes how systems are designed in the first place.

chapters.title: Consent and purpose

slide.heading: Lawful use and purpose
points: Use data for a clear, legitimate purpose
Direct care: often implied consent within the care team
New purposes, such as research, need a fresh basis
Patients should be told how their data is used

narration: Data protection laws in many countries, including the Mauritian Data Protection Act, treat health data as a special category that needs extra protection. Our focus here is on the general principles.
The first principle is that data must be used for a clear, legitimate purpose that the patient has been told about. Using it for something quite different needs a fresh justification.

For direct care, sharing within the care team is usually based on implied consent or on the law, because a patient who sees a doctor expects the nurse and pharmacist to see the relevant parts of the record.
But using the same data for a new purpose, such as a research study or marketing, normally needs explicit consent or another specific legal basis, such as approval by an ethics committee.

Transparency supports all of this. Simple notices in waiting rooms and on forms should explain what is recorded, who may see it, and how patients can ask questions or raise concerns about their records.

chapters.title: Minimisation and need to know

steps.title: Share
steps.sub: Only the fields the recipient needs

narration: Data minimisation means collecting, showing and sharing only the data that is actually needed for the purpose, and keeping it no longer than necessary.
A physiotherapist planning knee exercises needs the surgery details, not the patient's full psychiatric history. A receptionist booking appointments needs contact details, not laboratory results.
Access control turns this into practice. Each user gets a role, each role sees what it needs, and the principle of least privilege means nobody gets more access than their job requires.
Minimisation applies to sharing too. A public health report on dengue cases needs counts by area and week, not names and addresses of every patient.
Minimisation also protects staff. The less unnecessary data appears on a screen, the less chance there is of an accidental disclosure to someone standing nearby.

chapters.title: Audit and accountability

slide.heading: Audit trails
points: Record who accessed which record, when and what they did
Review regularly, not only after complaints
Support investigation when something goes wrong

narration: Even with good access control, clinicians need wide access in emergencies, so we cannot block everything. That is why audit is the partner of access control.
An audit trail records who opened which record, when, from where, and what they did. Systems can flag unusual patterns, such as staff opening records of patients with the same surname.
Audit trails only work if someone actually reviews them and if staff know they exist. The knowledge that every access is logged is itself one of the strongest deterrents.
In our opening story, an audit review would show the nurse opened a record of a patient she was not caring for, allowing the hospital to act and to reassure the patient.

chapters.title: Recap

slide.heading: Key principles
points: Privacy is a right; confidentiality a duty; security a safeguard
Use data only for legitimate, explained purposes
Minimise what is collected, shown and shared
Control access by role and audit every access

narration: To recap, privacy, confidentiality and security are related but different, and good security alone does not guarantee privacy.
The core principles are a lawful purpose and appropriate consent, data minimisation, role-based access with least privilege, and audit trails that create accountability.
In the next reading we will see how these principles are built into real systems.

items.title: Access control, audit trails and consent in practice
objectives: Compare role-based access control with simpler approaches
Explain break-the-glass access and why it must be audited
Describe what an audit log records and how it is used
Distinguish consent models used in health information exchange
chips: What is break-the-glass access?
What does a FHIR AuditEvent record?
What is the difference between opt-in and opt-out consent?
items.body:
Privacy principles such as minimisation and need-to-know only protect patients when they are built into the everyday behaviour of information systems. This reading looks at three practical mechanisms: **access control**, which decides who may see what; **audit trails**, which record what actually happened; and **consent management**, which records what the patient has agreed to. We finish with a worked case from a hypothetical regional hospital.

## Access control

Access control answers the question: *is this user allowed to perform this action on this data right now?* Three ideas underpin it.

1. **Authentication** confirms who the user is, for example with a personal username and password, ideally backed by a second factor such as a code on a phone. Shared logins ("ward3nurse") destroy accountability and should never be used.
2. **Authorisation** decides what the authenticated user may do.
3. **Least privilege** means each user gets the minimum access their job requires.

### Role-based access control

Most EHRs use **role-based access control (RBAC)**. Permissions are attached to roles, and users are assigned roles.

| Role | Can view | Can create or edit |
|---|---|---|
| Registration clerk | Demographics, appointments | Demographics, appointments |
| Nurse | Demographics, problems, allergies, medications, vital signs, notes for patients on their ward | Vital signs, nursing notes |
| Doctor | Full clinical record for patients under their care | Diagnoses, orders, prescriptions, notes |
| Pharmacist | Allergies, medications, relevant results | Dispensing records |
| Data analyst | De-identified or aggregated data only | Reports |

RBAC is easy to manage because a new nurse simply receives the nurse role. Its weakness is that roles can be too broad: a doctor role that allows access to *every* patient in the country is far more than any doctor needs. Many systems therefore add **context**, such as the patient being on the user's ward or having an appointment in the user's clinic. This is sometimes called a care relationship check.

### Sensitive records

Some information deserves an extra layer of protection: mental health, sexual health, HIV status, termination of pregnancy, or the records of staff members and well-known people. Systems can mark these records or sections as restricted, so that even users with a general clinical role must give a reason before opening them.

## Break the glass

Health care cannot always wait for permissions. A patient may arrive unconscious at the emergency department of a hospital where they have never been treated. **Break-the-glass** access lets an authorised clinician override normal restrictions in an emergency. The user must state a reason, the access is granted immediately, and the event is logged and reviewed later. The design principle is simple: *never block urgent care, but always make exceptional access visible.*

## Audit trails

An audit trail (or audit log) is a tamper-resistant record of access to and changes in the record. A useful entry answers:

- **Who** acted (user identity and role)?
- **What** did they do (view, create, update, print, export)?
- **Which** patient and which data?
- **When** and **from where** (time, workstation or device)?
- **Why**, where a reason was given (for example a break-the-glass justification)?

FHIR includes an `AuditEvent` resource for recording such events in a standard form, and a `Provenance` resource for recording where a piece of data came from and who created it.

Audit logs are useful in three ways. They allow **investigation** when a complaint is made; **proactive monitoring**, where software flags unusual patterns such as staff viewing family members' records or a user exporting thousands of records at midnight; and **deterrence**, because staff who know every access is logged are far less likely to browse out of curiosity. Some health services let patients see a list of who has accessed their record, which builds trust.

## Consent in practice

Consent is not a single checkbox. Health systems use different **consent models** depending on the purpose of data use:

- **Implied consent** for direct care within the care team: a patient who attends a clinic reasonably expects the doctor, nurse and pharmacist to see relevant information.
- **Opt-out**: data is shared (for example into a regional shared record) unless the patient objects. This achieves high coverage but relies on patients being well informed.
- **Opt-in**: data is shared only if the patient actively agrees. This gives stronger control but lower participation.
- **Explicit consent for specific purposes**, such as joining a research study or allowing a third-party app to read one's results.

Whatever the model, consent should be **informed** (the patient understands what will happen), **specific**, **recorded**, and **revocable**. FHIR has a `Consent` resource that lets systems record a patient's choices in a computable way, so that an exchange service can check them automatically before releasing data.

> **Worked example: a hypothetical regional hospital**
>
> A thirty-four-year-old teacher is admitted with a severe depressive episode. Her mother works as a clerk in the same hospital's finance department.
>
> - **Access control:** the finance clerk's role gives no access to clinical records at all. The ward nurses can see the record because the patient is on their ward. The psychiatric notes are flagged as sensitive, so a doctor from another ward must give a reason to open them.
> - **Break the glass:** two nights later the patient is transferred to the medical ward after an overdose. The on-call doctor uses break-the-glass to see the psychiatric notes, entering the reason "acute admission, medication history needed". This is legitimate and is reviewed and closed the next morning.
> - **Audit:** the monthly audit report flags that a radiographer with no involvement in her care opened the record twice. The privacy officer investigates, finds curiosity browsing, and the hospital follows its disciplinary procedure and informs the patient.
> - **Consent:** before discharge the patient is invited to join a depression research registry. She declines; her choice is recorded, and her data is excluded from the registry extract.

## Key takeaways

- Access control combines authentication, authorisation and least privilege; shared logins undermine accountability.
- Role-based access control is common, but should be refined with care-relationship context and extra protection for sensitive records.
- Break-the-glass allows emergency access without delay, at the price of mandatory justification and review.
- Audit trails record who did what, to which record, when and why, and support investigation, monitoring and deterrence.
- Consent models range from implied consent for direct care to explicit opt-in for research; FHIR's `Consent` and `AuditEvent` resources support them technically.

## Check your understanding

1. Why should every member of staff have a personal login rather than a shared ward login?
*Answer:* Because audit trails can only hold people accountable if each action is linked to an identifiable individual.
2. What three things should happen when a clinician uses break-the-glass access?
*Answer:* They give a reason, access is granted without delay, and the event is logged and reviewed afterwards.
3. A patient's data is used in a research registry. Which consent model is usually appropriate, and why?
*Answer:* Explicit (opt-in) consent, or another specific legal basis such as ethics approval, because research is a new purpose beyond the direct care the patient originally expected.

modules.title: Module 4 · Privacy by design and applying it

items.title: Privacy by design: secondary use, de-identification and breaches
objectives: Explain primary and secondary use of health data
Distinguish de-identification, pseudonymisation and anonymisation
Recognise re-identification risk in small populations
Outline the steps of responding to a data breach
chips: What is pseudonymisation?
Why is re-identification a risk in Mauritius?
What should a clinic do first after a data breach?

chapters.title: Primary and secondary use
narration: So far we have mostly discussed data used for the care of the individual patient. We call that primary use. But health data is also valuable for many other purposes.
Secondary use includes research into which diabetes treatments work best, planning how many dialysis machines a region needs, monitoring the quality of care, and public health surveillance.
These uses can benefit everyone. But the patient did not come to the clinic to take part in research, so secondary use needs its own justification and extra safeguards.
The main safeguard is to strip away, as far as possible, the information that identifies individuals before the data leaves the care setting.

Public health surveillance is a special case. Reporting notifiable diseases such as dengue or tuberculosis is usually required by law, so it does not depend on individual consent, but it still follows minimisation.

chapters.title: De-identification and pseudonymisation

cards.label: Remove direct identifiers
cards.text: Names, ID numbers, phone numbers, addresses

cards.label: Generalise
cards.text: Age band instead of birth date, district instead of street

cards.label: Pseudonymise
cards.text: Replace identity with a code; key kept separately

narration: De-identification is the process of removing or altering information that identifies a person. The obvious step is removing direct identifiers such as names, national identity numbers and phone numbers.
Pseudonymisation replaces the identity with a code, such as patient number seven four two. The key that links the code back to the person is held separately and securely.
Pseudonymised data is still personal data, because someone with the key can re-identify it. It is useful for research that must follow the same patient over time.
Anonymisation goes further. The data is altered so that individuals can no longer be identified by any reasonable means, often by generalising details and publishing only aggregated counts.
In practice, analysts often receive pseudonymised data inside a secure environment, where they can run their analysis but cannot download the raw records.

chapters.title: The small-island problem

slide.heading: Re-identification risk
points: Indirect identifiers combine: age, village, occupation, rare diagnosis
Suppress small counts in published tables

note.text: Removing names is not the same as anonymising

narration: Removing names is not enough. Indirect identifiers, such as age, sex, village, occupation and date of admission, can combine to point to a single person.

In a small island state this risk is high. If a dataset shows a forty-two-year-old male fisherman from a small coastal village with a rare cancer, many people in that village would know exactly who he is.

So data custodians generalise details, for instance using five-year age bands and districts instead of villages, and suppress small numbers in published tables, such as any cell with fewer than five patients.
The safest approach is to assess the risk of re-identification for each release, considering who will receive the data and what else they might already know.

chapters.title: Privacy by design
narration: Privacy by design means building privacy into a system from the start rather than bolting it on afterwards. Let me illustrate with a hypothetical project.
Suppose a health centre wants a mobile app so diabetes patients can upload glucose readings as FHIR Observations to the clinic's server.
Privacy by design would ask: which data do we really need, which staff should see it, how is it encrypted on the phone and in transit, how is access authorised, and how is every access audited?

It would also ask how patients are told about the app, how they consent and withdraw, and how long readings are kept. Writing these answers down before launch is called a data protection impact assessment.
None of this needs to make the project slow. Asking these questions early is far cheaper than redesigning an app after patients have already started using it.

chapters.title: When things go wrong
narration: Despite best efforts, breaches happen: a laptop is stolen, an email with a spreadsheet goes to the wrong address, or ransomware locks a hospital's systems.
The response follows a clear sequence. First contain the breach, for example by revoking access or recalling the email. Then assess what data was involved, whose, and how serious the risk is.
Then notify, as the law requires, which usually means the data protection regulator within a short deadline and, where the risk to people is high, the affected patients themselves.
Finally, learn. Find the root cause, fix it, and share the lessons, without simply blaming individuals, so the same mistake is less likely to happen again.
Preparation matters. Teams that have a written breach plan, know who to call, and have practised the steps respond far faster and cause less harm.

chapters.title: Recap

slide.heading: Key points
points: Secondary use needs its own basis and safeguards
Pseudonymised data is still personal data
Design privacy in; contain, assess, notify, learn after breaches

narration: To recap, secondary use of health data brings big benefits but needs its own justification, de-identification and careful risk assessment, especially in small populations.
Privacy by design builds minimisation, access control, audit and transparency into systems from day one, and a clear breach response limits harm when things go wrong.
You are now ready for the privacy quiz and for the final assignment, which brings records, FHIR and privacy together.

questions.q: A ward clerk with a valid login opens a celebrity patient's record out of curiosity. Which statement is most accurate?
o: No breach occurred because the login was valid
Security worked but privacy and confidentiality were breached
This is only a security failure
It is acceptable if the information is not shared
questions.ex: Having a valid login does not create a legitimate need to know, so privacy and confidentiality were breached even though security controls functioned.

questions.q: Which example best illustrates data minimisation?
o: Sending a public health team weekly dengue counts by district rather than patient names
Keeping all records forever in case they are useful
Giving every doctor access to every record nationally
questions.ex: Minimisation means sharing only the data the purpose needs; aggregated counts are enough for surveillance.

questions.q: Under role-based access control, what should a registration clerk normally be able to see?
questions.ex: Least privilege gives clerks only the data needed to register and book patients.

questions.q: An unconscious patient arrives at an emergency department where they have no care relationship. What is the appropriate mechanism?
o: Use a colleague's login with wider rights
Deny access until the patient wakes
Break-the-glass access with a reason, logged and reviewed
questions.ex: Break-the-glass gives immediate emergency access while ensuring justification and later review.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an audit trail in an EHR?
o: To record who accessed or changed which record, when and why
To store backup copies of results
questions.ex: Audit trails create accountability by recording access and changes, supporting investigation and deterrence.

questions.q: A research dataset replaces names with study codes, and the key is held by the hospital. How should it be classified?
questions.ex: Because the key allows re-identification, pseudonymised data remains personal data.

questions.q: A published table shows one patient aged 40 to 44 with a rare cancer in a small village. What is the best action?
o: Publish it, since names are removed
Add the patient's initials for accuracy
Suppress or combine small cells to reduce re-identification risk
questions.ex: Small counts in small populations can identify people, so they should be suppressed or aggregated.

questions.q: An email containing a spreadsheet of patient results is sent to the wrong address. What should the clinic do first?
o: Contain the breach, for example by recalling the email and asking the recipient to delete it
Wait to see if anyone complains
questions.ex: Breach response starts with containment, followed by assessment, notification and learning.

items.title: Assignment: Designing a privacy-aware FHIR data flow for a diabetes clinic

assignment.brief:
Scenario (hypothetical): A public area health centre in the south of Mauritius runs a weekly diabetes clinic for about 400 patients. The Ministry wants to pilot a link between the centre's EHR, the regional hospital laboratory and a patient mobile app, so that HbA1c and blood glucose results reach the clinic automatically and patients can upload home glucose readings. Aggregated data will also be sent to the national non-communicable disease programme.

Task: Write a briefing report (1,500 to 2,000 words, excluding tables, JSON and references) for the clinic's management committee that:
1. Describes the EHR components the clinic needs for this service (identity, problem list, medications, results, decision support and others) and how data flows between them during a typical diabetes review.
2. Explains, at a high level, how HL7 FHIR would support the exchange: name the resources you would use (at least Patient, Encounter and Observation), describe the RESTful interactions involved (for example, the laboratory creating an Observation and the app searching for a patient's results), and include one annotated FHIR Observation in JSON for an HbA1c result with a LOINC code, a reference to the patient and a UCUM unit.
3. Applies health-data privacy principles: a role-based access table for at least four roles, how data minimisation applies to the national programme extract, how consent will be obtained and recorded for the app, and what audit and break-the-glass arrangements are needed.
4. Identifies three key risks (technical, organisational or privacy) with a mitigation for each, and gives a short recommendation.

Deliverables: one PDF report with headings, at least one diagram or table of the data flow, the annotated JSON example, and a reference list of at least four sources (course materials may be cited). All patients and figures must be fictional; never include real patient data. Data provided: none beyond this scenario; state any assumptions you make.

rubric.desc: Accurately identifies the relevant EHR components and explains a clear, realistic data flow for a diabetes review, supported by a diagram or table.
Selects appropriate FHIR resources, describes RESTful interactions correctly, and provides a valid, well-annotated Observation in JSON with LOINC code, patient reference and UCUM unit.
Applies consent, minimisation, role-based access with least privilege, audit and break-the-glass specifically to the scenario, with a sensible access table and justified choices.
Identifies three credible risks with practical mitigations and a clear, well-argued recommendation.
Well-structured report for a non-technical committee, within the word limit, with clear tables and correctly formatted references.
